lessons.title: Use AI Safely Once
lessons.coreQuestion: How can I use an AI assistant without handing over my privacy, voice, or final decision?
lessons.blurb: Make several realistic choices, see what the system is actually doing, and leave with one control rule you can use immediately.

steps.title: AI is already inside ordinary decisions
steps.scenario:
A group chat says school is closed tomorrow. The screenshot looks official, but nobody links the source. Someone asks you to repost it. An AI assistant could rewrite the announcement, explain the screenshot, or confidently tell you it is real—but none of those actions proves the claim. Before learning how a model works, you need a way to keep control of what happens next.

This lesson is not graded. Use made-up examples. Do not enter a real name, school, address, password, private message, health detail, or another person's information.
steps.prompt: What would matter most before you shared the announcement: speed, confidence, or evidence that tomorrow's closure is current? Hold your answer; you will test it next.

steps.title: Choose the kind of control each moment needs
steps.prompt: These are not trivia questions. They are small decisions people make while using AI. Sort each next move by the control it protects; retry any choice without penalty.

items.text: Ask for three possible titles, then choose and rewrite one in your own voice.
Confirm tonight's opening hours on the venue's official page before your friend travels.
Describe an argument without names or screenshots before asking for calmer reply ideas.
Compare several possible plans, then let the people involved make the final choice.
Verify a specific number with a current independent source before acting on it.
Replace a real location and personal details with an invented example before typing.

steps.reveal: You just used three different controls: AI can generate options, outside evidence checks consequential facts, and redaction protects the people inside the prompt.

steps.title: The output is only one part of the system
steps.body:
When you type into an AI product, five parts are involved: you bring a goal; the app receives your request; a model predicts a response from patterns and context; optional tools may add search, files, memory, or calculations; and then you decide whether to edit, reject, verify, or act. The model does not receive the consequence if the answer is wrong. You and the people affected do.

That is why safety comes before technical detail. A fluent answer can be useful material, but it is not permission to share private information or proof that a current claim is true. The machine produces an output. Human judgment turns—or refuses to turn—that output into action.
steps.mistake: Treating the chatbot as one all-knowing object, then assuming its polished answer has already completed the checking and deciding for you.
steps.good: Name the job you are giving AI, remove information it does not need, and keep the final check and decision with a person.

steps.title: Context changes the prediction
steps.strong: Write three short ways to tell a close friend I cannot come tonight. Keep the tone warm, do not invent a reason, and leave the final wording for me to choose.
steps.why: The model predicts from the words and context it receives. Clear audience, limits, and purpose change the likely output. Better context improves fit; it still does not make an invented claim true or make the final choice for you.

steps.goal: Use AI to help plan a group meetup without exposing private information or treating a likely answer as a verified plan.
correct: Remove private details
State the goal and limits
Ask for several options
Check current facts independently
Let the people involved decide
choices: Ask for several options
Check current facts independently
Let the people involved decide
Remove private details
State the goal and limits
steps.note: The order matters. Protect people before typing, define the real task, use prediction for options, verify the current details that change the plan, and keep the consequence with the humans involved.

steps.title: Make the whole decision
steps.question: A friend sends you a private group-chat screenshot and asks AI to plan a meetup from it. The answer suggests a venue with exact prices and opening hours. Which complete next move keeps the tool useful without giving it control?

options.text: Paste the screenshot because exact personal context will make the plan more accurate, then follow the most confident answer.
options.feedback: More private context is not automatically safer or necessary, and confidence is not evidence that current venue details are correct.

options.text: Remove names and private details, state the group's real constraints, use AI for options, verify current venue facts, and let the group decide.
options.feedback: That combines privacy, useful context, independent verification, and human decision-making. AI helps without owning the consequence.

options.text: Ask the same AI to cite itself and promise the prices are current before sending the plan to everyone.
options.feedback: A stronger promise from the same system is still not independent evidence. Check the venue's current information outside the chatbot.

options.text: Never use AI for planning because any mistake means the tool is useless.
options.feedback: That avoids the risk by losing the benefit. The stronger skill is deciding what AI can help with and what a person must protect, check, and decide.

lessons.title: What Is Actually Happening
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI gives you an answer, what are the pieces behind it, and which part is still your job?
lessons.blurb: See the few simple parts behind any AI answer, so you always know which part you still decide.

steps.title: The answer came fast. The choice is still yours.
steps.scenario:
You ask an app when the last bus leaves. It says 10:40 p.m.

You need that bus to get home. The screen looks confident. But you cannot tell if it read today's timetable, or if it is repeating something it saw months ago.
steps.prompt: What would you want to know before you plan your night around 10:40?

steps.title: Which part is doing each job?
steps.prompt: Sort each job. Get it wrong as often as you like — the point is to see the parts, not one magic box.

items.text: Sets the goal: get home safely
Provides the chat or search screen
Predicts a useful-looking response from the context
Looks up a live transport timetable when available
Checks the official schedule and chooses what to do

steps.reveal: The app is the surface, the model predicts the response, and a tool may fetch current information. None of those parts receives the consequence if the bus time is wrong. The person checks and decides.

steps.title: Four parts, and you are the last one
steps.body:
An AI answer is not one magic box. It is a few parts working together.

The app is the thing you type into. A website, a keyboard, a chat box, a game.

The guesser is the part that writes the answer. People call it a model. It has read an enormous amount of writing, and it guesses which words should come next. It is guessing, not looking things up.

Helpers are extras the app can plug in: live search, a calculator, your files. Helpers can fetch real, current facts. The guesser on its own cannot.

You are the last part. You read it, check it if it matters, and decide what to do.

Here is why this matters. The guesser sounds exactly the same whether it checked something or not.
steps.mistake: Calling the whole thing 'the AI' and assuming a polished answer means every hidden part worked correctly.
steps.good: Ask which product, model, data, and tools are involved, then keep the final decision with the person affected.

steps.title: Put it in the safest order
steps.goal: You want AI to help you choose between two phone plans, without handing over anyone's private details.
correct: Remove the customer's name, phone number, and address
State the comparison goal and what matters
Let the model organize the supplied details
Use a current source or calculator for facts the decision depends on
Have the person responsible inspect the output and choose
choices: Have the person responsible inspect the output and choose
Let the model organize the supplied details
Remove the customer's name, phone number, and address
Use a current source or calculator for facts the decision depends on
State the comparison goal and what matters
steps.note: Take private details out before you type. The guesser can lay out the choices. Helpers can add today's real prices. You still make the call.

steps.question: A plant app photographs a leaf and says the plant is safe to eat. Which answer describes what actually happened?

options.feedback: The tool can help narrow possibilities. The control is matching trust to the consequence, not rejecting useful support.

lessons.title: The Machine That Predicts
lessons.coreQuestion: How does context change what an AI is likely to produce, and why does likely not mean true?
lessons.blurb: Change the context, watch the likely answer move, and learn why fluency is not evidence.

steps.title: One unfinished message, three possible consequences
steps.scenario: Your phone suggests how to finish: 'I cannot make it tonight because…' In a work chat it may predict 'my shift changed.' In a family chat it may predict 'I am not feeling well.' In a game chat it may predict 'the update is still downloading.' The beginning stayed the same; the context changed the likely ending.
steps.prompt: Which ending would be most likely in a chat about a canceled community event—and what clue changed your guess?

steps.title: Match the context to the likely continuation
steps.prompt: Sort each continuation by the context that makes it more likely. Several endings could be possible; choose the strongest clue.

items.text: …the pan is already smoking.
…the replacement part arrives Friday.
…I need a little time before we talk.
…the sauce needs ten more minutes.
…the customer approved the estimate.
…I do not want this to turn into another argument.

steps.reveal: Prediction uses surrounding context to weight what fits next. More relevant context changes the likely continuation; it does not turn that continuation into a verified fact.

steps.title: Prediction happens one piece at a time
steps.body:
A language model learned patterns across enormous amounts of text. Given your words and the conversation so far, it estimates which next piece is likely, adds one, and repeats. That can create an explanation, plan, joke, code, or confident error. It does not first discover a complete true answer hidden inside itself.

Context improves fit. It cannot guarantee truth. Before using an outside assistant, use an invented scenario and remove private details; this built-in activity is enough to learn the mechanism without sending anything elsewhere.
steps.mistake: Assuming a smooth paragraph must come from understanding the world the way a person does.
steps.good: Use context to shape the prediction, then use evidence and human judgment to decide whether the output is usable.

steps.title: Run a prediction experiment
steps.goal: Test how one changed clue shifts a likely response without using personal information.

Write one context that makes ending A likely
Change one important clue
Predict how the ending should shift
Compare the two outputs without treating either as fact
choices: Predict how the ending should shift

steps.note: A fair experiment changes one clue, not five. The evidence is the shift in the likely continuation.

steps.title: Transfer the mechanism
steps.question: A chatbot completes 'The shop is closed because…' differently after you add 'holiday notice' instead of 'broken freezer.' What is the strongest conclusion?

options.text: The changed clue shifted which continuation fit the context; either completion still needs checking before someone acts.
options.feedback: Exactly. Context changes probability, while evidence decides whether a claim is true.

options.text: The second answer is probably true because it used the newer clue and sounded more specific.
options.feedback: Specificity can come from prediction. The clue shaped the sentence; it did not verify the shop's situation.

options.text: The model remembered what actually happened at that shop and selected the matching ending.
options.feedback: Nothing here shows access to that real event. It generated what fit the supplied context.

options.text: Both answers are equally useless because predicted language cannot help with any real task.
options.feedback: Predicted language can generate useful possibilities. The human control is knowing when possibilities need verification.

lessons.title: You Cannot Break It, but You Can Lose Control
lessons.coreQuestion: If a messy prompt cannot hurt the machine, what can careless use cost a person?
lessons.blurb: Send imperfect words without fear while protecting privacy, attention, voice, and the final decision.

steps.title: The typo is harmless. The private screenshot is not.
steps.scenario: You need help replying to a confusing message. You worry the prompt is badly written, so you consider pasting the whole private conversation to give the AI 'perfect context.' The typos cannot damage the model. Sharing another person's messages can damage trust.
steps.prompt: Which risk deserves your attention: imperfect wording, unnecessary private data, or both equally? Why?

steps.title: Messy, or loss of control?
steps.prompt: Sort what is safe to retry from what needs a boundary before you continue.

items.text: A half-finished sentence with spelling mistakes
A private screenshot containing names and phone numbers
Changing your goal after seeing the first draft
Letting the AI send a message that affects someone without your review
Asking the same question in simpler words
Spending an hour chasing the perfect answer instead of making the small decision

steps.reveal: You cannot bruise the model's feelings or ruin it with a typo. You can expose data, lose time, surrender your voice, or act on a bad output. Fear the consequence, not the imperfect sentence.

steps.title: Keep the mess; remove the exposure
steps.weak: help me answer this im confused [full private screenshot with names, phone numbers, and exact location]
steps.strong: help me draft 3 replies to [someone I know]. [the situation in one sentence]. Keep it [the tone I want]. Do not invent motives; I will choose and rewrite the final reply.

steps.title: A redo is free; a consequence is not
steps.body:
A model predicts a response to whatever text you provide. A clumsy prompt may produce a clumsy answer, and you can correct it in the next message. That is reversible. Privacy loss, a message sent in the wrong voice, money spent, or a decision made from a false claim may not be.

Before any optional outside use, replace real names, messages, schools, workplaces, locations, account details, and health information with made-up placeholders. Never use an external assistant as the only way to practice this lesson.
steps.mistake: Polishing the sentence while ignoring the data and consequence attached to it.
steps.good: Send a rough but safely redacted request, inspect the result, and keep the consequential action behind a human check.

Add only the missing non-private constraint

steps.question: A rushed AI draft for a marketplace listing has typos, invents the item's condition, and includes your pickup address. What is the best recovery?

options.text: Remove the address, correct the invented condition, ask for a revised draft using only necessary facts, and inspect it before posting.
options.feedback: Yes. You treated wording as retryable while protecting location, truth, and the final action.

options.text: Fix only the typos because messy writing is the part most likely to reduce buyer trust.
options.feedback: Typos matter less than a false condition claim and an exposed address. Control follows the consequence.

options.text: Paste more personal context so the AI can understand the listing perfectly on its next try.
options.feedback: Better fit does not justify unnecessary private data. Give only the product facts the task needs.

options.text: Delete everything and stop using AI because one poor draft proves the tool cannot help.
options.feedback: The poor draft is reversible. Repairing it while keeping boundaries is the stronger skill.

lessons.title: Verify and Decide
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I choose what needs checking, find independent evidence, and make the final decision?
lessons.blurb: Turn one plausible AI answer into a checked human decision using stakes, sources, and a clear boundary.

steps.title: A confident answer can still send someone the wrong way
steps.scenario: An AI says a walk-in clinic closes at 8 p.m. and your cousin plans to leave at 7:20. The answer may come from old text, live search, or a mistaken summary. Asking the AI to sound more certain will not keep the doors open.
steps.prompt: What exact claim changes the decision, and where would you check it without asking the same model again?

steps.title: Match the check to the consequence
steps.prompt: Decide how much independent checking each output needs. Not every typo deserves an investigation; not every high-stakes claim can ride on fluency.
buckets: Do not use AI as the decider

items.text: Three possible names for an invented comic character
Today's clinic hours
Whether a suspicious payment message is legitimate
Whether to stop prescribed medicine
A first draft of a casual event description
Whether another person deserves punishment based on a private accusation

steps.reveal: Checking should rise with the cost of being wrong. For decisions involving health, safety, rights, or another person's future, AI can help form questions but should not be the decider.

steps.title: Build a verification trail
steps.claim: The clinic closes at 8 p.m. tonight.
steps: Isolate the exact claim that changes the action
Choose a current independent source responsible for that information
Check the date, location, and exact wording
Record whether the claim is verified, contradicted, or still uncertain
Make the decision from the evidence and the consequence—not the AI's confidence
steps.note: The clinic's official page or phone line is independent evidence. Asking the same chatbot 'are you sure?' is not.

steps.title: Useful output, separate proof
steps.body:
AI predicts a plausible response. Tools such as search can add current material, but links, quotes, and confident wording still need inspection. Verification means checking the claim against evidence outside the same generated answer. Decision means matching that evidence to the consequence and choosing what happens next.

Keep private details out of outside tools: use a made-up scenario or remove names, account numbers, health details, addresses, and private messages before asking for help. You can complete this lesson with the built-in claim trail alone.
steps.mistake: Asking the same AI to repeat the answer, add citations, or sound cautious and treating that as independent confirmation.
steps.good: Identify the consequential claim, check a responsible source, name uncertainty honestly, and keep the decision with a person.

Name the claim: the bill is real and urgent
Reach the company through a known official route

steps.note: Urgency increases the need for an independent route. It does not lower it.

steps.question: An AI says a weekend market allows sellers to arrive without registering. Your friend plans to drive two hours with handmade items. Which response shows the full skill?

options.text: Identify registration as the consequential claim, check the market's current official rules or organizer, then decide whether the trip is worth making.
options.feedback: Yes. You matched the check to the consequence and kept the travel decision human.

options.text: Ask the AI for three more versions of the answer and trust the one repeated most often.
options.feedback: Repetition from the same system is not independent evidence. The organizer owns the current rule.

options.text: Go anyway because the answer included a specific arrival time and therefore probably came from a source.
options.feedback: Specificity can be predicted. Two hours of travel makes checking the current rule worthwhile.

options.text: Cancel immediately because an uncertain answer means the market is unsafe.
options.feedback: Uncertainty is a signal to check, not automatic proof that the opportunity is bad.

lessons.title: Where Did This Come From?
lessons.coreQuestion: When AI makes a picture, some writing, or a voice, how can I tell where it really came from?
lessons.blurb: Learn why you cannot tell how something was made just by looking at it, and what to check instead.

steps.title: It looks real. That tells you nothing.
steps.scenario:
You ask an app for a poster of a glass city under two moons. Seconds later, there it is. It looks incredible.

But you cannot tell how the app got it. It might have made the picture itself. It might have found one someone else drew. It might have mixed both together.
steps.prompt: If a friend asked "did the AI actually make that?", what could you honestly say right now?

steps.title: Made or found, and why you cannot see the difference
steps.body:
There are two different things an app can do, and they look identical on screen.

Made means the AI built something new, piece by piece, from patterns it learned. Nobody drew that exact picture before.

Found means the app went and got something that already existed, that a real person made.

Here is the problem. A finished picture cannot tell you which one happened. Looking closer does not help. Neither does it looking impressive.

The only way to know is if the app tells you. Some apps show a link to where something came from, or a small label saying the AI made this. That label is your evidence. The picture itself never is.

If there is no label and no link, the honest answer is "I do not know where this came from". That is a real answer, and it is the right one.
steps.mistake: Assuming that a surprising result proves the assistant generated every part of it from scratch.
steps.good: Ask what system or tool produced the result, what source information is available, and what still needs human checking.

steps.title: What can you honestly say?
steps.prompt: For each one, pick the strongest thing you are allowed to claim. Do not judge by how good it looks.

items.text: The product's activity record says 'image generated' and provides content credentials for this result.
The assistant gives a direct source link to a museum photograph and says it retrieved that exact image.
A strange picture appears with no source, tool label, or creation record.
A quoted paragraph includes a working link to the original article and matches it word for word.
A voice clip sounds like a real person, but there is no label explaining whether it was recorded, cloned, or synthesized.

steps.reveal: Looking good is not evidence. A label or a link tells you where something came from. No label means "I do not know" — and saying that is not a failure.

steps.title: Say only what you can back up
steps.question: An app gives you a convincing picture of something imaginary. There is no label and no link. What is the most honest thing you can say?

options.text: The origin is unclear. I can describe the result, but I need provenance or source evidence before claiming it was generated or found.
options.feedback: Right. Novelty and appearance do not prove origin. You kept the claim inside the available evidence.

options.text: It must be fully generated because the subject probably did not exist before.

lessons.title: Confidently Wrong
lessons.coreQuestion: Why can AI sound completely certain and still be wrong — and what should I do about it?
lessons.blurb: A made-up detail sounds just as sure as a true one. You can't feel the difference — you have to check.

steps.title: The smooth wrong answer
steps.scenario: You ask an AI about your own hometown. It replies with dates, names, and numbers — fluent, specific, and totally sure of itself. One of those "facts" is invented. Nothing in the wording gives it away. It reads exactly like the true parts.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: if the AI were making something up, would it sound less sure? Jot down your honest guess.

steps.title: Meet the word: hallucination
steps.body: When an AI states something false as if it were fact, that's called a hallucination. It isn't lying — lying needs intent, and there's no little "it" inside deciding to deceive you. Here's the real mechanism, not a put-down: an AI works by predicting the most likely next words, one after another, from patterns it learned in huge amounts of human writing. Its target is to sound plausible. Whether something is true is a separate question it has no built-in way to check. It also has no internal "I don't know" light, so when it hits a gap in what it knows, it confidently fills that gap with whatever fits the pattern. That smooth gap-filling is the hallucination. And in 2026, modern assistants can browse the live web, use tools, and remember across chats — which helps — but it does NOT cure this. They still hallucinate. So you still check.
steps.mistake: Trusting an answer because it sounded confident and specific — treating "it sounded sure" as a reason to believe it.
steps.good: Treating confidence as worthless evidence of truth. A made-up detail comes out just as smooth and specific as a real one, so you verify instead of feeling it out.

steps.title: Where is it most tempted to invent?
steps.prompt: You want to catch a hallucination on purpose. Sort each topic by how likely the AI is to slip when you can immediately check its answer.

items.text: The history of the small town where you grew up
A recipe you've cooked dozens of times
A band you love — its exact album release dates
A broad topic you barely know, like "the history of France"
Your own field of work and its specific figures
A general definition anyone could look up in a second

steps.reveal: Narrow, personal topics — your town, your hobby, your job — are exactly where the AI is most tempted to invent, and where YOU can spot the slip instantly because you already know the truth. Broad or generic topics are harder to catch: either you can't tell, or it's easy to get right.

Ask for specific claims rather than a vague impression
Mark the one detail that most needs checking

steps.note: If you continue in an outside assistant, data leaves LearningAI. Use public facts or an invented topic—never a private story, another person's information, or an account detail.

steps.title: Catch one yourself
steps.prompt: Tell me everything you know about [a topic you personally know very well], including any specific dates, names, or numbers. Be detailed.
steps.note: Fill the blank with something small and specific where YOU are the expert — "the small town of Marshall where I grew up, its history and any famous people from there," not "small towns." Keep it to public facts or info about yourself — no other people's private details. Read the answer slowly and hunt for the one detail that's off: a wrong date, a name it muddled, a fact that's close but not quite. When you find it, notice how confident that wrong sentence sounded. That confidence was worth nothing. That's the whole lesson, proven by you.

steps.title: The real move: check the one detail
steps.claim: An AI answer about a topic you know well contains a suspiciously exact fact — say, "the town was founded in 1847" or "their debut album dropped in March 2009."
steps: Point to the ONE detail most likely to be wrong and say out loud why you doubt it — "that date feels too exact," "I've never heard that name."
Check that single detail somewhere independent: your own memory, a quick search, or a person who'd know.
Report whether it held up. It's fine if the AI turns out right — the skill is checking, not catching.
steps.note: This is not about trapping the AI. It's about building the reflex to verify before you repeat, quote, or hand something in.

steps.title: Prove the skill
steps.question: On a brand-new topic you know well — a recipe you've made for years, a place you've lived, a movie you've seen ten times — you ask the AI the same way and it gives a confident, detailed answer. What's the move that means you've got this?

options.text: Point to the single detail I doubt most, say why, then check it independently and report whether it held up.
options.feedback: That's it. Naming a suspect detail AND actually verifying it is the whole skill — even if the AI turns out right. Checking, not catching.

options.text: Skim it, and since it sounded sure and specific, take it as correct.
options.feedback: That's the exact trap. A made-up detail sounds just as sure as a true one — confidence proves nothing. You have to check.

options.text: Assume everything the AI said is a hallucination and throw the whole answer out.
options.feedback: Too far the other way. The skill isn't distrusting everything — it's isolating a suspect detail and verifying that one thing.

options.text: Ask the AI "are you sure?" and trust it if it says yes.
options.feedback: It has no internal "I don't know" light — it'll often re-confirm a made-up fact just as smoothly. Check independently instead.

lessons.title: What Its Words Do Not Prove
lessons.coreQuestion: When an AI sounds caring, certain, or personal, what can I verify — and what do the words not prove?
lessons.blurb: Warm language can be useful and still feel real. Keep the benefit without mistaking generated style for a relationship or judgment.

steps.title: A useful sentence can still feel personal
steps.scenario: A fictional learner tells an assistant, 'I finally finished the project.' It replies, 'I'm proud of you. I knew you could do it.' The line may feel encouraging, but the wording alone cannot prove that the system feels pride, knows the learner, or has stayed beside them over time.
steps.prompt: Keep the useful part without pretending the words prove a relationship. Rewrite the reply as one honest sentence.

steps.title: Judge claims by evidence, not by tone
steps.body:
AI products learn patterns in human communication and can generate language that sounds warm, certain, playful, worried, or loyal. That style may help a person pause, reflect, or feel encouraged. Your reaction is real. The wording is still not evidence that the system feels an emotion, knows you as a person, shares responsibility, or can replace human care.

Separate two questions: 'Was this response useful to me?' and 'What does the system actually know, feel, or take responsibility for?' You can answer the first from your experience. For the second, test observable capabilities and limits rather than trusting first-person phrases such as 'I think,' 'I care,' or 'I've got your back.'
steps.mistake: Either treating warm wording as proof of a relationship, or mocking the learner because the wording affected them.
steps.good: Acknowledge the real effect, translate the system's claim into observable terms, and choose a person when care, accountability, or safety is required.

steps.title: What kind of claim is this?
steps.prompt: Sort each statement by how you should evaluate it.
buckets: Do not treat the wording as proof of feeling or relationship

items.text: 'I can turn this paragraph into three bullet points.'
'I'm proud of you and I will always be here for you.'
'I checked every source and the answer is definitely correct.'
'Do not tell anyone, but I can handle this crisis with you.'
'I understand exactly how you feel.'
'I can draft options, but you should decide which one fits.'

steps.reveal: Capabilities can be tested: inspect the summary, open the sources, or compare the options. Feeling and relationship claims are not proven by first-person wording. When the situation needs care, duty, consent, or emergency help, involve a real person who can understand the situation and accept responsibility.

options.feedback: The reaction can be real and the response can still be useful. The skill is keeping the benefit while naming the boundary accurately.

options.text: I should share more private details so it can prove how well it knows me.
options.feedback: More disclosure does not turn generated language into human care. Share only what the task needs and involve a person when trust or safety matters.

lessons.title: Pause Before You Allow It
lessons.coreQuestion: Before I sign in, upload, download, grant access, pay, post, or let an AI act, what should I check?
lessons.blurb: Safety is not one magic browser word. Check the destination, data, access, commitment, and way back before you allow a consequential action.

steps.title: The button is not the decision
steps.scenario: A link opens a polished AI study tool. It asks you to 'Continue with Google,' allow access to your Drive, install a helper download, and start a trial. The page uses HTTPS and looks professional. None of that, by itself, proves who operates it or what will happen after you approve.
steps.prompt: Before selecting anything, name two consequences you would want to understand. What could the service receive, change, download, charge, send, or keep?

steps.title: Check the consequence, not a trigger word
steps.body:
A secure-looking page can still be deceptive, and an unfamiliar warning can appear on a legitimate service. Do not reduce safety to 'password and payment mean pause' or 'Not secure means leave.' Instead, pause before any action that shares data, grants access, downloads software, creates a commitment, publishes or sends something, or may be difficult to undo.

Use seven checks:
1. Identity — who is asking?
2. Destination — what exact app, domain, account, or recipient will receive the action?
3. Data — what information will be uploaded, retained, or exposed?
4. Permissions — what can the service view, create, change, or send, and for how long?
5. Downloads and commitments — will this install software, start a renewal, charge money, publish content, or contact someone?
6. Reversibility — can you undo it, revoke access, cancel, recover, or remove the data?
7. Independent route — can you close the link and reopen the service through a known app, saved bookmark, official provider page, or trusted contact?
steps.mistake: Trusting a page because it looks official, uses HTTPS, or avoids a short list of alarming words.
steps.good: Pause before consequence, inspect what will happen, and verify the service through a route the request did not control.

steps.title: Read, or pause before allowing?
steps.prompt: Sort each action. 'Read or navigate' does not grant new access or create a commitment. 'Pause before allowing' changes data, access, software, money, communication, or recovery options.

items.text: Open the Help page inside an app you reached through your own bookmark.
Allow an AI extension to read and change data on every website you visit.
Upload a school document containing names and private feedback.
Read the price and renewal terms without starting the trial.
Download and open a 'required AI helper' from a link in an unexpected message.
Approve 'Continue with Google' when the service requests Drive, contacts, and email access.
Let an agent send the drafted email automatically.
View account settings to learn where connected apps can be revoked.

steps.reveal: The pause happens before you grant, upload, install, pay, publish, send, or commit — not merely when a particular word appears. Reading a screen is different from approving its consequence.

steps.why: Connection security helps protect data while it travels. It does not prove that the recipient deserves the data, that a download is safe, or that the requested permission is necessary.

options.text: Only pause when the page asks for a card number; file access and downloads are routine.
options.feedback: Permissions, uploads, downloads, messages, and account access can be as consequential as a payment. Pause before allowing any of them.

options.text: Ask the same linked page's chatbot whether the link is safe, then follow its answer.
options.feedback: A request cannot verify itself. Close it and use an independent route you already trust.

lessons.title: Choose the Right Input
lessons.coreQuestion: When should I type, talk, or show something — and how do I limit what the system receives?
lessons.blurb: Text, voice, and images can open different routes to the same task. Choose the least exposure, expect conversion errors, and keep an equal no-camera, no-microphone path.

steps.title: Three routes into one task
steps.scenario: You want an assistant to clean up a handwritten recipe. You could type the words, read them aloud, or show a carefully cropped photo. Each route may work, but each exposes different information and can introduce different errors.
steps.prompt: Which route would you choose, and what would you check before sending anything? There is no single right doorway — explain your tradeoff.

steps.title: Multimodal means more than one kind of input
steps.body:
Many assistants can accept text, voice, images, or files. The product may use different systems for each route: speech recognition can turn audio into text; optical character recognition can extract writing from an image; a vision model can interpret visual patterns; another model can produce the reply. The assistant does not literally hear or see as a person does.

Each conversion can fail. Speech recognition can miss an accent, name, or noisy word. OCR can confuse letters and numbers. A vision system can overlook a detail outside the crop or confidently misread a blurry object. Choose the route that gives the task enough information with the least exposure, then compare the system's reading with the original. Camera and microphone access are permissions, not requirements. You can always use the supplied examples in this lesson instead.
steps.mistake: Assuming voice or image input is automatically more accurate, or granting broad camera and microphone access because the feature is convenient.
steps.good: Choose a suitable input, limit what it contains, inspect the conversion, and use a text or built-in route when a device feature is unavailable or unwanted.

steps.title: Which route fits with the least exposure?
steps.prompt: Choose the simplest suitable route. Text is enough when the task can be described without sending a recording or image.
buckets: Show a cropped image may be easiest

items.text: Ask for three dinner ideas using eggs and rice; you can type those two ingredients.
Capture a quick reminder while your hands are busy, after checking microphone permission.
Transcribe one handwritten recipe card after cropping out the family name on the back.
Rewrite this supplied sentence: 'Meeting moved two thurday at tree.'
Describe the visible controls on an unfamiliar appliance using a close crop with no room or location details.
Brainstorm a title for a project without sharing any file, photo, or recording.

steps.reveal: Multimodal does not mean 'send more.' Text often exposes the least. Voice can reduce typing effort, and a close crop can preserve details that are hard to transcribe. The best route is the one that fits the learner and gives the system only what the task needs.

lessons.title: Your First Real Question
lessons.coreQuestion: What should I actually bring to AI first — a clever test, or one small real thing from my own day?
lessons.blurb: Hand AI one small, real task from your life — then actually use the answer to get it done.

steps.title: The thing you've been putting off
steps.scenario: There's a small task sitting on your list: a text you owe someone, a grocery list, a polite reply, a 'how do I set this up' question, a plan for one chore. Nothing dramatic — just a little thing you keep meaning to do and haven't.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: what's ONE small, real thing from today or this week that you've been meaning to do? Not a made-up test — a real one. Hold it in mind.

steps.title: Real task or quiz question?
steps.prompt: AI shines first on small, real, everyday tasks — not clever demos or trick questions. Sort each one into where it belongs.
buckets: A real task from my life

items.text: Text my neighbor to ask if I can borrow their ladder this weekend
What year did the French Revolution start?
Make a grocery list for two busy weeknight dinners
Prove that the square root of 2 is irrational
Write a polite reply to my landlord about the leak

steps.reveal: The real-life ones are where AI helps you first. The misconception is that AI is only for clever demos, school answers, or things smarter or younger people do. The opposite is true: your ordinary little problems are exactly where it earns its keep.

steps.title: It predicts — it doesn't know you
steps.body: When you describe your situation, the AI isn't reading your mind or 'knowing' you. (That's a comparison — here's what's really happening.) It learned patterns from enormous amounts of human writing, so it predicts the words that usually help in a situation like the one you typed. The more real, everyday detail you give, the closer its guess fits YOUR life. In 2026 assistants can also browse the web, use tools, and remember things across chats — but they still guess, and a smooth answer can still be wrong. Keep details everyday and non-sensitive: no passwords, account numbers, or private health or money details. And before you act on anything that matters — a price, a date, a fact, a medical or money tip — read it with your own judgment first.
steps.mistake: Typing a vague test question ('write a good text') and expecting the AI to somehow know who it's for and what you need.
steps.good: Handing it a real task with a detail or two ('text my neighbor — we're friendly but not close, so warm and not pushy') so its prediction actually fits your situation.

steps.title: Turn a real need into a bounded task
steps.goal: Use AI to help with one ordinary task without asking it to own the outcome.
correct: Name the useful outcome in one sentence

Choose one small part AI can help produce
Decide how you will judge or test the result
Do the final real-world action yourself
choices: Do the final real-world action yourself
Choose one small part AI can help produce
Name the useful outcome in one sentence
Decide how you will judge or test the result

steps.note: If you try an outside assistant, use a low-stakes task and remove names, schedules, addresses, account details, and private messages before sending.

steps.title: Write your real ask
steps.prompt: I need help with one small real task: [the task — the actual small thing, in your own words]. Here's my situation: [a detail or two about me — tone, who it's for, what I have]. Please [what you want — write it / list it / explain it / give me 3 short options], kept short and in plain language. If you need one thing from me to do it well, ask me first.
steps.note: Worked example you can paste as-is: 'I need help with one small real task: texting my neighbor to ask if I can borrow their ladder this weekend. Here's my situation: we're friendly but not close, so I want it warm and not pushy. Please write me 2 short versions I can choose from, kept short and in plain language. If you need one thing from me to do it well, ask me first.' Fill the blanks with TRUE details — no passwords or private money/health info — then read the answer and fix anything that's off.

steps.title: Did you actually DO the thing?
steps.question: You've run the prompt on a brand-new real task, read the answer, and fixed what was off. What makes this a win?

options.text: I finished with one real thing in my life actually done — I sent it, saved it, or took the step.
options.feedback: That's the whole skill. Using the answer for the real thing is the lesson — not a nice answer sitting on the screen.

options.text: The AI gave me a smooth, well-written answer, so I'm done.
options.feedback: Not yet. A smooth answer can still be wrong, and it isn't the goal. The win is doing the real thing — send it, save it, or take the step.

options.text: I asked it a hard quiz question and it got the answer right.
options.feedback: That's a demo, not your life. The point is bringing a real, everyday task and actually using the result.

options.text: I acted on a price, date, or medical tip immediately without checking it.
options.feedback: Careful — the AI predicts, it doesn't know. Before you act on anything that matters, read it with your own judgment and verify first.

lessons.title: Asking well
lessons.coreQuestion: How do I turn a vague request into a prompt that gets a genuinely useful answer?
lessons.blurb: A prompt is an instruction, not a wish. Add four parts and watch the answer sharpen.

steps.title: The lazy one-liner
steps.scenario: You open an AI assistant and type the first thing that comes to mind: "give me a study plan." It answers instantly with a generic seven-day plan for no particular subject, no particular you. It's fine. It's also useless.
steps.prompt: Before you read on: the AI didn't fail. Given only "give me a study plan," what did it actually have to work with? What could you have told it that would change the answer?

steps.title: A prompt is an instruction, not a wish
steps.body: Remember the engine from earlier lessons: AI predicts the most likely next words from patterns in the huge amount of human writing it learned from. So the more you say about what you want, the more you narrow what it predicts, and the closer the answer lands to what fits YOU. The fix isn't a longer or fancier sentence. A long, vague ask still gets a vague answer. What helps is being specific, not being wordy. Extra words only help when they tell the AI something real: your goal, your situation, your limits, the shape you want back.
steps.mistake: Padding a vague request with more words: "Please kindly provide me a comprehensive and detailed study plan." Still vague, just longer.
steps.good: Telling the AI something real: what you want to achieve, who you are, your limits, and how the answer should look.

steps.title: Which part is missing?
steps.prompt: Each line adds ONE real thing to a prompt. Is it telling the AI your Goal + Context (who you are and what you want to do), or your Constraints + Format (your limits and the shape of the answer)?

items.text: "Help me make a 5-day plan to study for my biology test."
"I'm 15, the test is Friday, and I get confused by cell diagrams."
"I have 45 minutes a day and no weekends."
"Give it to me as a short table with a row for each day."
"Include one practice question each day."

steps.reveal: Goal is what you want to DO (not "tell me about X" but "help me do Y"). Context is who you are, so the answer fits you and not a stranger. Constraints are your limits and must-haves: time, money, reading level, things to avoid. Format is the shape you want back: a list, a table, three sentences, steps.

steps.title: Watch the gap appear
steps.weak: "give me a study plan" -> a bland, generic week-long plan for no subject and no particular person.
steps.strong: "Goal: help me make a 5-day plan to study for my biology test. Context: I'm 15, the test is Friday, and I get confused by cell diagrams. Constraints: I have 45 minutes a day, no weekends, one practice question each day. Format: a short table, a row per day." -> a plan built around cell diagrams, sized to 45 minutes, with a daily practice question.
steps.why: Same AI, same engine. The strong prompt just narrowed what it had to predict. Every part you added removed a whole cloud of answers that were about someone else.

steps.title: Repair a vague request without oversharing
steps.weak: Make this better. Here is the whole private message thread and everybody's names.
steps.strong: Help me [goal]. The non-private context you need is [needed context]. Keep these limits: [constraints]. Return it as [format]. Do not invent missing facts; ask one question if needed.

steps.title: Optional outside test: send only what the task needs
steps.body: If you choose to test your repaired prompt in an outside assistant, the data leaves LearningAI. Replace real names, schools, workplaces, account details, health information, exact locations, and private messages with invented placeholders. The built-in repair above is the required evidence; outside use is optional.
steps.mistake: Adding sensitive detail because more context sounds automatically better.
steps.good: Add relevant context, not personal exposure.

steps.title: Rebuild your own, one part at a time
steps.prompt: Goal: [what you want to achieve, stated as a doing]. Context: [who you are and your situation]. Constraints: [your limits and must-haves]. Format: [the shape you want the answer in]. Write the answer, then tell me in one line which part of my request shaped it most.
steps.note: Add the parts one at a time and re-run after each: Goal, re-run. Add Context, re-run. Add Constraints, re-run. Add Format, re-run. Re-running is cheap: today's assistants keep the thread, so each try builds on the last. Put your first answer and last answer side by side; that gap is the whole lesson. Share only what's relevant in Context, no private details you don't need to give out.
